putra
(‘one who saves [the ड़थेर् from the हेल्ल् called] pum’)
------------------------------------------
The desire for a worthy son (or sons) is a universal phenomenon noticed in almost all societies, ancient or modern. The Hindus believed that he would save the ड़थेर् from a special kind of हेल्ल् called ‘pum’. Hence the name ‘putra’. A son born from a sacramentally and legally sanctioned मर्रिअगे, as per the dictates of the धर्मशास्त्रस्, was called ‘aurasa-पुत्र,’ a son born out of one’s own bosom.
These धर्मशास्त्रस् describe twelve kinds of sons, many of whom have been considered as illegitimate. Only the औरस and the दत्तक (adopted son) are legally eligible for recognition.
If it was the duty of the parents to bring up the son by giving him proper एदुचतिओन्, training and culture, it was equally the latter’s duty to take care of them while living and perform all the obsequial rites properly after their death.
As regards the इन्हेरितन्चे of the parental property by the sons, some of the धर्मशास्त्रस् (Manusmṛti 9.112; Yājñavalkyasmṛti 2.114) gave a greater portion to the eldest son, though many others recommended that it be distributed equally among all the sons.
It was the duty of the sons, especially the eldest one, to take care of the parents.

Putrakāmeṣṭi
(‘a [Vedic] sacrifice [to be performed by] one desiring for a son’)
------------------------------------------
The desire for a worthy son is a natural phenomenon in all the societies of the world; more so in the ancient Hindu society. Understanding this, the ṛṣis of yore had prescribed a particular Vedic sacrifice called ‘Putrakāmeṣṭi’ or ‘Putreṣṭi’ for the fulfilment of this desire.
King दशरथ is said to have performed it on the advice of the sage Ṛṣya-śṛṅga (vide रामायण, Bālakāṇḍa 15).
The king performed the अश्वमेध-याग first, to purify himself and then only the पुत्रकामेष्टि.
The Rāmāyaṇa says that the mantras were taken from the Atharvaśiras (vide Bālakāṇḍa 15.2 and 3). The Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtras also describes it.
However, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to get the details.

putrikā
(‘daughter treated like a son’)
------------------------------------------
When a person has only one putrī or daughter and no sons, he can ceremonially adopt her as a son. Then she is called ‘putrikā’.
Alternatively, she can be given in मर्रिअगे to a suitable bridegroom under the condition that her son will be adopted by him (the ड़थेर् of the girl) as his own son. In this case, the boy may be called ‘putrikāputra’. However, this latter word may also mean पुत्रिका herself.
Such a daughter is entitled to perform all the obsequial rites of her parents, just like a son.
